title: Evaluating an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM-Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). The preregistered paired design used N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine). A single shared initial candidate was generated per task by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and presented to both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks and could trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode when validator.violation_count>0. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120 (1.00); guarded success = 120/120 (1.00). Contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We incorporate clarifications grounded in the archived execution artifacts (model configuration, task manifest, scoring JSONs, analysis logs) and provide expanded methodology, execution accounting, representative diagnostics, and limitations.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language intent into concrete network configuration commands, enabling faster NetOps workflows. However, syntactically plausible commands can nonetheless violate workflow policies (e.g., requiring an interface to be administratively down before changing MTU), break availability invariants (e.g., both uplinks down during a switchover), or cause regressions. A common mitigation is to place verification or emulation-based validators between generation and enactment and to allow bounded repair iterations when violations are found. Prior work advocates such guarded architectures but often evaluates end-to-end systems where generation and validation effects are conflated.

We conducted a preregistered, artifact-rich, paired experiment to isolate the marginal effect of an executable validator and a single-step repair mechanism on identical generator outputs. The preregistered research question (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) asks: Does integrating an executable emulator validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To answer this precisely we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: for each task the same generation was supplied to both conditions, so any difference arises only from validation/repair. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment with complete execution and analysis artifacts archived; (2) empirical execution accounting showing a concordant-ceiling outcome on the curated task bank; (3) artifact-grounded diagnostics demonstrating validator trace structure and repair conditioning; and (4) a methodological discussion of design choices, statistical degeneracy, and recommendations for future confirmatory tests.
sections.related_work:
Evaluations of LLM-driven NetOps commonly expose failure classes not visible from text-level correctness checks. Recent executable benchmarks and testbeds (e.g., NetConfArena and related emulation-grounded suites) emphasize closed-loop testing to reveal semantic failures arising during enactment. Prior tool papers and surveys propose generate→validate→repair loops, veto layers, canary deployments, and model→formal-model translation as practical guardrails; these works show that external verification or emulation can reduce semantic errors in representative scenarios. However, published studies often vary generators, validators, and prompting simultaneously, which complicates attribution.

Our study complements this literature by fixing the generator and isolating the validator/repair stage via a paired, shared-generation design. This design answers a different, mechanistic question than multi-component comparisons: does a validator/repair subsystem improve outcomes when the generator output is held constant? The preregistered experiment and its degenerate result demonstrate how paired shared-generation designs can produce uninformative nulls when the generator already satisfies encoded semantic checks. The broader literature also documents gaps motivating our approach: scarcity of production-rooted misconfiguration corpora, limited multi-model comparisons under identical harnesses, and under-explored methods for calibrated uncertainty on structured outputs—issues we address in our reproducible archival practice.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 and archived before execution. The preregistration specified a paired-binary design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks, deterministically assigned into three topology classes (edge, core, leaf–spine) with 40 tasks each. Each task yields one shared initial candidate produced by the declared generator (requested_model = "gpt-5-mini") and evaluated under two conditions: baseline (LLM-only suggestion semantics, synthetic-apply) and guarded (generate→validate→repair pipeline). The preregistration is referenced in archival manifests and preregistration_sha256 is recorded in the execution manifest.

Generation stage: The hosted model declared in execution/model_configuration.json is gpt-5-mini; execution accounting records model_calls_used = 120 and stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 120. The incarnation of the generation stage used deterministic seeds and a single initial-generation call per pair (initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1) according to the preregistered execution_contract. The shared-generation constraint (independent_condition_generation = false) enforces identical generator outputs across conditions.

Validator and repair: The guarded pipeline used a deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, validator_version = 5.0) that implements intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks encoded in each task manifest (examples: must_be_down_for_fields, make-before-break patterns, group-activity constraints). The preregistered repair policy allowed ≤1 repair iteration and required repair_applied only when validator.violation_count>0; repair prompts and repair traces would be archived when used. The scorer applied a full_intent_constraint_validation rule and produced per-episode validator_trace artifacts containing validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied fields. Representative scoring JSONs in execution/scoring/ illustrate these structured fields.

Task generation and difficulty labels: The task bank was produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry contains an explicit required_sequence (the correct operation ordering), initial_state, expected_final_state, and metadata fields (difficulty level, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count). These metadata permit stratified analyses by topology and difficulty in future experiments.

Statistical estimand and analysis plan: The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (per-pair reduction in emulator-observed semantic-failure rate). The prespecified confirmatory test is the exact two-sided McNemar; complementary reporting includes the paired-difference point estimate and a bootstrap-percentile 95% confidence interval using 10,000 resamples and bootstrap_seed = 1729. The preregistered primary analysis uses complete pairs only; technical/instrumentation failures were to be excluded and logged with reasons for sensitivity analyses. All analysis steps and parameters were recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed the planned episodes (planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240) and produced a single shared initial generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline = 120 successes, 0 failures and guarded = 120 successes, 0 failures (success_rate = 1.0 for both conditions). analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv shows a contingency of n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 120 and zero technical/instrumentation exclusions.

Per-topology outcomes: Tasks were deterministically assigned 40 per topology. Aggregated per-topology success counts from archived artifacts are: Edge: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Core: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Leaf–spine: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40. These per-topology counts are reconstructed from execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/.

Representative validator traces and repair activity: Representative scoring JSONs (for example, execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) show normalized_response matching normalized_reference_answer, parsed_command_count = required_command_count, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, and validator_trace.repair_applied = false. Across the archive validator.violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes; consequently no repair_provider_trace artifacts were produced and the preregistered secondary endpoints regarding repair frequency are vacuous for this run.

Confirmatory statistics and degeneracy: With zero discordant pairs the exact two-sided McNemar p-value equals 1.0 and the paired-difference estimate is 0.00. The preregistered bootstrap-percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) returns [0.00, 0.00]. This degenerate zero-width CI is an expected statistical artifact: bootstrapping an empirical paired table that contains no discordant observations reproduces identical resampled contingency counts across resamples, yielding a pointwise degenerate interval. The analysis/analysis_log.jsonl records these bootstrap parameters and the paired-analysis completion event.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the concordant-ceiling outcome: The shared-generation paired design isolates validator/repair effects by presenting identical generator outputs to both conditions. In this specific task bank and under the archived generator/prompting configuration, every shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic emulator validator's encoded intent and workflow policies, producing a concordant-success ceiling (n_11 = 120). Under such conditions the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair behavior and therefore could not reduce semantic failures relative to baseline. The observed McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.00,0.00] are consistent statistical reflections of this ceiling.

Methodological implications: The paired shared-generation design answers a precise mechanistic question—does validation/repair improve outcomes for identical generator outputs—and the present answer for the curated corpus and declared generator is "no effect" because the generator produced only valid candidates. This narrow null should not be conflated with a broader claim that validators are unnecessary: in practice, independent generation variability, prompt perturbations, alternative model families, or adversarial inputs may produce invalid candidates for which validation and repair could be decisive. The archived task metadata (difficulty, dependency counts) enables stratified future designs that allow independent per-condition generation to measure practical repair utility.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is supported by deterministic reconciliation artifacts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) and provider-call audit logs showing hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and no cache reuse. Construct validity is limited by the deterministic emulator's operationalization of semantic correctness via task-encoded workflow policies—some production failure modes may be absent. External validity is constrained by synthetic task provenance and single-model scope (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini); multi-vendor heterogeneity and partial observability in live networks are not represented. Conclusion validity is impacted by the ceiling outcome: preregistered power assumptions (target absolute reduction = 0.15) are not applicable when the baseline success rate is already 100% on the curated set.

Operational implications and reproducibility: The run demonstrates an artifact-grounded integration pattern: structured validator traces (validation_before/after, touched_field counts, violation lists) support operator-facing explanations and post-hoc audits even when the validator is unused. Deterministic harness artifacts—task manifests, scoring JSONs, provider-call audits, and deterministic-reconciliation outputs—are archived and allow independent replay of the exact confirmatory run. Future operational evaluations should vary generation independence, increase repair budgets, test multiple generator models and prompt perturbations, and extend validator fidelity to multi-vendor behaviors to more directly assess practical repair value.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment (N=120) that compared an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling effect on this curated synthetic task bank and clarifies that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear when generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design can cleanly isolate validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts support reproducible failure analyses even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. We supply comprehensive archived artifacts so follow-up studies can relax shared-generation constraints, vary generators and prompt perturbations, and evaluate repair budgets against more production-rooted corpora.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
